claim: The embryonic midgut of Drosophila is composed of muscle cells ensheathing an endodermal layer, linked by extracellular matrix.
source: The embryonic midgut – composed of muscle cells ensheathing an endodermal layer, linked by extracellular matrix (Figure 1A) – offers a system in which we can overcome these challenges and probe in toto organ dynamics across tissue layers at sub-cellular resolution.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the anatomical composition of the embryonic midgut.

claim: Hox genes expressed in the muscle layer are required for the midgut to form its four chambers.
source: Hox genes expressed in the muscle layer are required for the midgut to form its four chambers, but the mechanism by which genetic expression patterns are translated into tissue deformation, and in turn to organ shape, remains unclear (Figure 1B–C; Bienz, 1996; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Wolfstetter et al., 2009; Bienz and Tremml, 1988; Immerglück et al., 1990; Reuter and Scott, 1990; Panganiban et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Dynamic, high-frequency calcium pulses drive patterned muscle contraction, inducing convergent extension in the endoderm to sculpt stereotyped folds.
source: We find that dynamic, high-frequency calcium pulses drive patterned muscle contraction, inducing convergent extension in the endoderm to sculpt stereotyped folds.
evidence: This is a primary finding statement summarizing the main discovery of the study.

claim: The midgut is a closed tube by stage 15 of embryonic development, residing 20–60 μm below the embryo surface.
source: The midgut is a closed tube by stage 15 of embryonic development, residing 20–60 μm below the embryo surface (Bate and Martinez Arias, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The organ first constricts halfway along its length, then constricts again to subdivide into four chambers.
source: The organ first constricts halfway along its length, then constricts again to subdivide into four chambers (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Video 1 showing the developmental process.

claim: Within 75–90 min after the onset of the first fold, the constrictions are fully formed, and the organ beings to adopt a contorted shape.
source: Within 75–90 min after the onset of the first fold, the constrictions are fully formed, and the organ beings to adopt a contorted shape.
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the study's data.

claim: The surface area of the midgut grows by approximately 30% during folding (stages 15-16a).
source: We find that gut morphogenesis is stereotyped and exhibits reproducible stages (Figure 1E). The surface area grows by ∼30% during folding (stages 15-16a) and remains constant by the time constrictions are fully formed (16b), despite continued shape change.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The enclosed volume within the midgut decreases only gradually during morphogenesis.
source: The enclosed volume within the midgut decreases only gradually during this process, while the effective length of the organ – the length along its curving centerline – triples (Figure 1E, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The effective length of the organ triples during morphogenesis.
source: The enclosed volume within the midgut decreases only gradually during this process, while the effective length of the organ – the length along its curving centerline – triples (Figure 1E, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: As constrictions develop, endodermal cells lose their anisotropy and even become elongated along the AP axis in posterior regions.
source: As constrictions develop, cells loose this anisotropy and even become elongated along the AP axis in posterior regions (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell shape measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cell shape change is not due to rotations of cells.
source: Measurement of endodermal cell orientations reveal that this effect is not due to rotations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by orientation measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cell areas in the endoderm change only gradually during morphogenesis.
source: Despite the large changes in aspect ratio, cell areas in the endoderm change only gradually (Figure 2E), such that cells converge along the circumferential axis while extending along the folding longitudinal axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There are no signs of cell division during midgut morphogenesis.
source: However, we find no signs of cell division during this process, confirming previous observations (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' observations and a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalations are not significantly biased in orientation during early stages of constriction.
source: Moreover, although tracking quartets of cells in the anterior midgut revealed widespread intercalations (also called T1 transitions), the orientations of these events were not significantly biased for the early stages of constriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Anisotropic cell shape change may be the primary contributor to tissue-scale shape change.
source: This suggests that anisotropic cell shape change may be the primary contributor to tissue-scale shape change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of cell divisions and unbiased intercalations.

claim: The midgut tissue is thin compared to the organ radius.
source: Given that the midgut tissue is thin compared to the organ radius, cells exert forces on one another primarily through in-plane interactions, but in-plane mechanical stress can couple to curvature to generate out-of-plane motion (Arroyo and Desimone, 2009).
evidence: This is a geometric observation about the tissue structure, with a citation to theoretical work.

claim: In-plane mechanical stress can couple to curvature to generate out-of-plane motion.
source: Given that the midgut tissue is thin compared to the organ radius, cells exert forces on one another primarily through in-plane interactions, but in-plane mechanical stress can couple to curvature to generate out-of-plane motion (Arroyo and Desimone, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: The pattern of out-of-plane deformation almost entirely accounts for in-plane dilatational motion in the gut.
source: Remarkably, we find that the pattern of out-of-plane deformation almost entirely accounts for in-plane dilatational motion in the gut, with only a small change in local tissue areas (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Video 5.

claim: In-plane divergence and out-of-plane deformation are correlated at the 97% level.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, these terms match with 97% correlation, leaving a residual in-plane growth residue at the level of ∼1% per minute.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The tissue behaves as an incompressible medium.
source: This tight link suggests that the tissue behaves as an incompressible medium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tight correlation between out-of-plane and in-plane motion.

claim: Slow residual area growth is primarily concentrated in the lobes of rounding gut chambers.
source: This slow residual area growth, which is primarily concentrated in the lobes of rounding gut chambers, accounts for the surface area growth noted in Figure 1E and the cellular area growth in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is an observation linking different measurements in the study.

claim: Embryos with disrupted muscle structure fail to fold.
source: It is known that embryos with either disrupted muscle or endoderm structure fail to fold (Bilder and Scott, 1995; Singer et al., 1996; Wolfstetter et al., 2009; Wolfstetter et al., 2017), as do embryos lacking integrins linking the two layers (Devenport and Brown, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Embryos with disrupted endoderm structure fail to fold.
source: It is known that embryos with either disrupted muscle or endoderm structure fail to fold (Bilder and Scott, 1995; Singer et al., 1996; Wolfstetter et al., 2009; Wolfstetter et al., 2017), as do embryos lacking integrins linking the two layers (Devenport and Brown, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Embryos lacking integrins linking muscle and endoderm layers fail to fold.
source: It is known that embryos with either disrupted muscle or endoderm structure fail to fold (Bilder and Scott, 1995; Singer et al., 1996; Wolfstetter et al., 2009; Wolfstetter et al., 2017), as do embryos lacking integrins linking the two layers (Devenport and Brown, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gut morphogenesis requires an interaction between muscle and endodermal layers.
source: This suggests that gut morphogenesis requires an interaction between muscle and endodermal layers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing that disruption of either layer or their connection prevents folding.

claim: Hox genes are expressed exclusively in the muscle layer.
source: At the same time, hox genes – which are expressed exclusively in the muscle layer – have been linked to the successful formation of specific folds (Figure 4A–B; Tremml and Bienz, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 4.

claim: Antp mutants lack the anterior constriction.
source: In particular, Antp mutants lack the anterior constriction lying near the center of the Antp domain (Figure 4C), while Ubx mutants lack the middle constriction lying at the posterior edge of the Ubx domain (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ubx mutants lack the middle constriction.
source: In particular, Antp mutants lack the anterior constriction lying near the center of the Antp domain (Figure 4C), while Ubx mutants lack the middle constriction lying at the posterior edge of the Ubx domain (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Genetic patterning of the endoderm occurs via genetic patterning from the muscle layer.
source: In this system, genetic patterning of the endoderm occurs via genetic patterning from the muscle layer (Bienz, 1996; Mendoza-Garcia et al., 2021), so it is possible that constrictions result from a genetic induction process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Muscle and endoderm layers move together, with initially close nuclei separating by approximately 5 μm per hour.
source: By tracking both circumferential muscle nuclei and endoderm nuclei in the same embryo, we find that these two layers move together, with initially close nuclei separating by ∼5 μm per hour (Figure 4E–F, Video 6, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 4E-F and supplementary figures.

claim: The two layers are tightly tethered by integrins and extracellular matrix binding the heterologous layers.
source: This result is consistent with the notion that the two layers are tightly tethered by the integrins and extracellular matrix binding the heterologous layers (Devenport and Brown, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed tight coupling, supported by a citation.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of muscle contractility using CRY2-OCRL driven by Antp-GAL4 reliably prevented anterior constrictions.
source: Driving CRY2-OCRL with Antp-GAL4 under continuous activation of blue light reliably prevented anterior constrictions (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Driving CIBN and CRY2-OCRL under continuous blue light activation in muscle regions posterior to the anterior fold using Ubx-GAL4 M1 locally inhibited constriction dynamics.
source: Likewise, driving CIBN and CRY2-OCRL under continuous blue light activation in muscle regions posterior to the anterior fold using Ubx-GAL4 M1 locally inhibited constriction dynamics.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Inhibiting contraction in selected regions mimics the genetic mutants known to remove folds.
source: Inhibiting contraction in selected regions therefore mimics the genetic mutants known to remove folds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of optogenetic and genetic mutant phenotypes.

claim: Optogenetic activation using the CIBN UAS-RhoGEF2 system in the Antp region generates an anterior fold on demand on the timescale of a few minutes.
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation using the CIBN UAS-RhoGEF2 system in the Antp region generates an anterior fold on demand on the timescale of a few minutes, even if induced long before the constriction would normally begin (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Activation of the Ubx-GAL4 M1 domain results in a nearly uniform constriction that dramatically alters the shape of the organ.
source: Similarly, activation of the Ubx-GAL4 M1 domain results in a nearly uniform constriction that dramatically alters the shape of the organ, forcing the yolk to flow into the anterior chamber.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Muscle contractility is necessary for constrictions.
source: We conclude that muscle contractility is necessary for constrictions and inducing contraction and the associated downstream behaviors is sufficient to generate folds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Inducing muscle contraction is sufficient to generate folds.
source: We conclude that muscle contractility is necessary for constrictions and inducing contraction and the associated downstream behaviors is sufficient to generate folds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of muscle contractility significantly reduced endodermal cell shape change.
source: In contrast to wild-type, optogenetic inhibition of muscle contractility significantly reduced endodermal cell shape change.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: The endodermal program of convergent extension is induced by mechanical interaction with the contracting muscle layer.
source: Thus, the endodermal program of convergent extension is induced by mechanical interaction with the contracting muscle layer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic and mutant experiments.

claim: Calcium signaling triggers muscle contractions in a wide range of contexts.
source: Recent studies have shown that calcium signaling triggers muscle contractions in a wide range of contexts (Kuo and Ehrlich, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dynamic calcium pulses appear in the muscle layer in regions localized near all three midgut constrictions.
source: As shown in Figure 5A–E and Video 7, dynamic calcium pulses appear in the muscle layer in regions localized near all three midgut constrictions.
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Video 7.

claim: Calcium pulses are patterned in time, appearing only at the onset of constriction for each fold.
source: Additionally, these calcium pulses are patterned in time, appearing only at the onset of constriction for each fold (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Antp mutants, calcium activity was almost entirely absent during stages 15–16.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, we found that calcium activity was almost entirely absent during stages 15–16.
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s measurements in Antp mutants shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Calcium pulses continue to appear at the anterior constriction in Ubx mutants.
source: In contrast, calcium pulses continue to appear at the anterior constriction in Ubx mutants, suggesting local control of calcium pulses by Antp in the anterior constriction (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s measurements in Ubx mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hox gene Antp is upstream of dynamic calcium pulses.
source: The hox gene Antp is therefore upstream of dynamic calcium pulses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Antp mutants lack calcium pulses.

claim: In smooth muscle cells, calcium triggers muscle contraction by binding to calmodulin, which in turn binds to myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) to trigger myosin light chain phosphorylation.
source: In smooth muscle cells, calcium is known to trigger muscle contraction by binding to calmodulin, which in turn binds to myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) to trigger myosin light chain phosphorylation (Hill-Eubanks et al., 2011), and cytoplasmic calcium is transported from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for storage under regulation of SERCA (Kuo and Ehrlich, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on calcium signaling mechanisms.

claim: Cytoplasmic calcium is transported from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for storage under regulation of SERCA.
source: In smooth muscle cells, calcium is known to trigger muscle contraction by binding to calmodulin, which in turn binds to myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) to trigger myosin light chain phosphorylation (Hill-Eubanks et al., 2011), and cytoplasmic calcium is transported from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for storage under regulation of SERCA (Kuo and Ehrlich, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on calcium regulation.

claim: Spatially localized calcium dynamics – under the control of hox gene patterning – triggers MLCK signaling leading to muscle contractions.
source: From this we infer that spatially localized calcium dynamics – under the control of hox gene patterning – triggers MLCK signaling leading to muscle contractions (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic, optogenetic, and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Convergent extension and sharp folds in the endodermal layer are triggered by mechanical interaction of muscle contractility together with tissue incompressibility.
source: We found that convergent extension and sharp folds in the endodermal layer are triggered by mechanical interaction of muscle contractility together with tissue incompressibility, and patterns of calcium signaling regulate contractility in muscle cells according to hox-specified information (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Patterns of calcium signaling regulate contractility in muscle cells according to hox-specified information.
source: We found that convergent extension and sharp folds in the endodermal layer are triggered by mechanical interaction of muscle contractility together with tissue incompressibility, and patterns of calcium signaling regulate contractility in muscle cells according to hox-specified information (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Calcium dynamics have known roles in early developmental stages of diverse organisms.
source: While calcium dynamics have known roles in early developmental stages of diverse organisms (Wallingford et al., 2001; Strutt, 2003; Li et al., 2019; Brodskiy et al., 2019) – including influencing the organization of muscle fibers in the midgut (Huycke et al., 2019) and determining cell fates in heart valves (Fukui et al., 2021) – our findings suggest a direct influence of calcium on shape, wherein pulses trigger a program of irreversible tissue deformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Calcium dynamics influence the organization of muscle fibers in the midgut.
source: While calcium dynamics have known roles in early developmental stages of diverse organisms (Wallingford et al., 2001; Strutt, 2003; Li et al., 2019; Brodskiy et al., 2019) – including influencing the organization of muscle fibers in the midgut (Huycke et al., 2019) and determining cell fates in heart valves (Fukui et al., 2021) – our findings suggest a direct influence of calcium on shape, wherein pulses trigger a program of irreversible tissue deformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Calcium dynamics determine cell fates in heart valves.
source: While calcium dynamics have known roles in early developmental stages of diverse organisms (Wallingford et al., 2001; Strutt, 2003; Li et al., 2019; Brodskiy et al., 2019) – including influencing the organization of muscle fibers in the midgut (Huycke et al., 2019) and determining cell fates in heart valves (Fukui et al., 2021) – our findings suggest a direct influence of calcium on shape, wherein pulses trigger a program of irreversible tissue deformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Calcium pulses trigger a program of irreversible tissue deformation.
source: While calcium dynamics have known roles in early developmental stages of diverse organisms (Wallingford et al., 2001; Strutt, 2003; Li et al., 2019; Brodskiy et al., 2019) – including influencing the organization of muscle fibers in the midgut (Huycke et al., 2019) and determining cell fates in heart valves (Fukui et al., 2021) – our findings suggest a direct influence of calcium on shape, wherein pulses trigger a program of irreversible tissue deformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Calcium-patterned muscle contractions control 3D shape through a mechanical cascade across tissue layers.
source: These calcium-patterned muscle contractions control 3D shape through a mechanical cascade across tissue layers, with broad relevance to tissue engineering and organ morphogenesis in other organisms.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings and their implications.

claim: The anterior fold forms near the center of the Antp domain.
source: For example, the anterior fold forms near the center of the Antp domain.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.
